indicators.label: Resting heart rate
indicators.plain: How fast your heart beats when you are fully at rest, usually measured during sleep.
indicators.how: Wear the wrist or chest sensor overnight. Keel takes the lowest stable stretch while you sleep, so exercise and coffee do not distort it.
indicators.why: A resting heart rate that climbs above your own normal is one of the earliest whole-body signs of infection, dehydration, poor recovery or loss of fitness.

indicators.label: Heart rate variability
indicators.plain: The small beat-to-beat changes in your heart rhythm (RMSSD). Higher usually means your body is recovering well.
indicators.how: Measured automatically overnight by the wearable, or in a two-minute still reading with the chest strap.
indicators.why: HRV drops when the body is under strain: illness, short sleep, heavy training or stress. It often moves before you feel anything.

indicators.label: Blood oxygen
indicators.plain: The share of your red blood cells carrying oxygen.
indicators.how: Overnight from the wearable, or a 30-second fingertip reading: warm hand, hold still, wait for a steady number.
indicators.why: A sustained drop can point to a breathing or lung problem or a cabin atmosphere issue.

indicators.label: Body temperature
indicators.plain: Your body temperature, from the wearable skin sensor overnight or a thermometer reading.
indicators.how: For a spot check use the thermometer at the same time each day, before exercise and before eating or drinking.
indicators.why: A rise above your own normal supports the picture of infection or inflammation; body temperature also runs differently in space.

indicators.label: Sleep duration
indicators.plain: Hours actually asleep in the last sleep period.
indicators.how: Measured by the wearable. If you did not wear it, enter your best estimate at check-in.
indicators.why: Crews sleep less in space than on Earth. Short sleep builds up as a debt that slows reactions and raises error risk.

indicators.label: Sleep timing shift
indicators.plain: How far the middle of your sleep moved from your scheduled sleep period. Zero means you slept when planned.
indicators.how: Calculated from when you fell asleep and woke up.
indicators.why: When sleep slides away from the schedule, your body clock and the mission clock disagree, which hurts sleep quality and alertness.

indicators.label: Exercise, 7-day average
indicators.plain: Average minutes of exercise per day over the last week.
indicators.how: Logged by the exercise devices or entered at check-in.
indicators.why: Daily exercise is the main protection against losing bone, muscle and heart fitness without gravity. Missed sessions add up quietly.

indicators.label: Reaction time
indicators.plain: Your average response time in the reaction self-test.
indicators.how: Tap as soon as the target appears. Do it at about the same time each day, sitting still, before caffeine if you can.
indicators.why: Reaction time is a sensitive, objective sign of fatigue. It slows with sleep loss and may slow with high cabin carbon dioxide.

indicators.label: Mood
indicators.plain: Your own rating of how you feel today, from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good).
indicators.how: Answer quickly and honestly at check-in. There is no right answer, and you decide who can see it.
indicators.why: Isolation, confinement and distance from home wear on everyone. A slow slide is easier to turn around when it is noticed early.

indicators.label: Fluid intake
indicators.how: Tap once per drink bag at check-in, or enter litres.
indicators.why: Crews tend to drink too little in space. Low intake raises the risk of kidney stones and makes the heart work harder.

indicators.label: Food intake
indicators.plain: How much of your planned food you ate today.
indicators.how: Estimate at check-in: all, most, about half, little.
indicators.why: Under-eating is common in space and speeds up loss of body mass, muscle and bone.

indicators.label: Body mass
indicators.plain: Your body mass, measured on the mass-measurement device (a normal scale does not work without gravity).
indicators.how: Weekly, same time of day, before eating.
indicators.why: Steady loss of body mass signals under-eating or dehydration.

indicators.label: Blood pressure (upper)
indicators.plain: The upper (systolic) number of your blood pressure.
indicators.how: Sit still for five minutes, cuff on the upper arm at heart level, do not talk during the reading.
indicators.why: Blood pressure regulation changes without gravity. Readings well outside your normal deserve a repeat and a word with the medical officer.

indicators.label: Blood sugar
indicators.plain: The sugar level in a fingertip drop of blood.
indicators.how: Clean fingertip, first drop wiped away, measure before breakfast for a comparable number.
indicators.why: Named in the challenge as a useful indicator. Keel shows it against your own previous readings and a general reference range.

indicators.label: Cabin carbon dioxide
indicators.plain: The average carbon dioxide level in the cabin air over the last day.
indicators.how: Read automatically from the cabin air monitor.
indicators.why: In a closed cabin, exhaled carbon dioxide builds up. Higher levels are linked to headaches and may dull thinking.

indicators.label: Radiation dose
indicators.plain: The radiation dose your personal dosimeter recorded today, and your running mission total.
indicators.how: Read automatically from your personal dosimeter. Keep it on you.
indicators.why: Beyond Earth's magnetic shield the crew receives a steady dose from cosmic rays and occasional bursts from solar storms. The total is tracked against a career limit.
